text: The main purpose of this Internship project called PixelProof is whether or not the detected photograph is AI generated or AI manipulated. This project contains two modules. First one is Module1. This module simply looks at the whole image and classifies this image as AI generated or real photograph. Second one is Module2. This module looks at spesific areas of the image and tries to detect AI touched areas but this module remains experimental. One of the major goals of this project is to avoid incorrect labeling, such as labeling real image as an AI generated image. Results of the project improved on the development data however, there are no gurantees that the result is fully trustworthy. The main result is a web demo which allows users to upload images supported by user friendly interface.

My Internship was from 20 July to 18 September, and there were 40 working days. This report will show you the process of the development of the project and the experiment, decision-making process. The sections in this report refer to different contents. For instance, section 2 is about Company introduction, section 3 gives information about the background of the project and problem description, section 4 discusses development of the project and its results, section 5 gives information about Internship experience, section 6 and section 7 are about conclusion and recommendations, section 8 contains references and section 9 includes appendices. Additionally, E92 refers to the number of experiments, and experiments are not conducted independently (Keleş, 2026).

Initial step was to prepare dataset which includes AI generated images and real images named CIFAKE. The dataset seperated into 3 groups train , validation, test. Next step was to train a CNN model (small CNN) and investigate the results. This model showed good performance in the test set and accuracy was 96,75% , but in a different dataset which does not include CIFAKE images, the performance of the model dropped and accurracy decreased to 77.1%. These experiments result indicate that different types of datasets, changes the model performance due to format, compression levels and size. After this inference, images were transformed into common format named JPEG and the test was conducted again. There was no clear drop in new test (Keleş 2026).

One of the main problems of this project was missclarification. This missclarfication includes two types. The first type is false positive which means that a real image is considered as AI generated . The second type is false negative which means AI generated images do not get regocnized by the model. There are some possible solutions , but there might be performance drop in other metrics. For instance, when more AI generated images are added and labled as ai generated, there might be performance increase in AI detection. However, detection of real images performance might drop down. An other factor is image features such as format, size, compression level. These factor may leed the model make mistakes. Therefore, these image features should optimized

The main motiviation of this project to build a system that help users to diffirentiate AI generated images from real images. Therefore, reducing the error rates was curricial. Optimization of the features is necessary. Also, the system has a web demo with user friendly UI
There are several related litarture that this project took advantage and these litaratures will be explained and they are realated for this project will be disscused.

Wang et al. (2020) explored that a model that learned images that generated from certain AI generator could detect other images that generated from different generaotrs this resarch is related since this project tries to detect images from various generators.

Ojha et al. (2023) studied how a pretrained vision model’s features could be used to detect AI generated images by adding a simple classifier. This is related to this project because some methods follow similar approaches.
CLIP could be considered as a feature extractor from images. Radford et al., 2021) . The Project used these extracted features to detect AI generated images.

DINOv2 is a pretrained model that learns features that could be used in different tasks, and this model does not need hand made class labels while learning (Oquab et al., 2024). Its relationship with this project is that features extracted from images by DINOv2 were used in training models that differentiate real and AI generated images.

According to Grommelt et al. (2024) model could learn image size or compress methods instead of AI traces. Therefore, this might produce misleading results. Relationship between this project is there are some findings that patterns of image size and compression methods could affect performance.

DEAR uses inpainting of a specific region of an image to examine the features and disscards some featurs in order to have stronger results (Kim et al., 2026). In this project this model should be examined carefully since capabilities of this model does not mean that these capabilities could help to solve our problem or enhance our results.

SIDD is a dataset which contains images from 10 different scenes taken with 5 different smartphone cameras. This might be valuable for this project because of camera diversity. However, this does not mean that there is a wide variety of scenes; on the contrary, scene diversity is limited (Abdelhamed et al., 2018).

The SID dataset has paired images that were captured using low light conditions RAW images (Chen et al., 2018). The use of SID in the current project made it possible to incorporate actual images captured in low light situations. Nevertheless, RAW images are processed under different conditions compared to JPEG images.

High score of the model does not mean that the result will have the same accuracy rate. Scores need to be examined carefully and some methods like calibration can make scores match actual accuracy better (Guo et al., 2017). In our web demo we cannot demonstrate the score as the probability of being AI generated. Also, choosing a threshold value does not mean transforming the score into a probability.

Guo et al. (2017) explain that a high model score does not always mean a high chance of being correct. Calibration helps confidence scores match actual accuracy better. In our web demo, the score is not shown as the probability of an image being AI generated. Choosing a threshold does not turn the score into a probability.

Dwork et al. (2015) explain that repeatedly using the same evaluation results to make changes can make those results less reliable as evidence of performance on new data. This is related to our project because some datasets were used several times during development. Therefore, an independent final test was still needed.

Adobe Content Credentials records information about where content comes from and how it was edited (Adobe, 2026). PixelProof follows a different approach by examining image pixels for AI traces. Checking Content Credentials was not implemented in this project.

section: 4.5.1 Early models and the first transfer failures:
text: The first model called small CNN trained with CIFAKE dataset which includes 90,000 training images, 10,000 validation images and 20,000 test images. Other model called ResNet-18 which is a pretrained model performed similar 97.66%. However, when dataset seperate data set which is consist of 995 images model performance drop down to 25.2%. The reason behind this was resolution problem. After fixing this problem performance largely regained.(Keleş, 2026, E1-E6).

section: 4.5.1 Early models and the first transfer failures:
text: After training the first models, next step fallowed by comparing several methods. Such as analyzing images in their original resolution, utilized features extracted from smaller image patches, use already trained detectors and combining model outputs. Some of these methods achived higher scores on certain datasets than others. However, in some cases error rates increased in both cases such as detecting real or genereted image. These controlled experiments leads us to give more importance to quality of the data and diversity and determining the creteria for models rather than looking camera noise or other features of image (Keleş 2026, E8-E50)

section: 4.5.1 Early models and the first transfer failures:
text: It turns out that before making a expensive change in a model data quality and status should be examined more comprehensively.

Noticing reverse labeling in two dataset which means real and AI generated images labelled opposite after correcting this labeling and repeating experiments scores of AUC of DINOv2 increased 0.480% to 0.764. Therefore, interpretation of unsuitableness of the model was wrong and using more training data decreased the false alerts compared to first calculations
In a different experiment, the threshold selection procedure can employ test data. This is similar to having access to the exam questions before sitting for the exam. Once this issue was fixed, the candidate model no longer satisfied the acceptance criteria and thus failed (Keleş, 2026, E19b-E19c and E27).
Reverse labeling may cause a model perfom bad in the task, therefore after correction experiments repated and recorded.

Parent means that initial image that there was no process applied by us. In E92 there were 7,674 real and 4,595 AI generated images in total 12,269. For each image 4 versions were created. First one is clear version, second one is imitating transport version, third one is compressed version JPEG with quality 75, fourth is reduced version with the longest edge at most 1080 pixels and compressed with JPEG quality 75. Therefore 49,076 image versions were obtained from 12,269 initial images.

Table 2 shows the datasets that were used in separate processes. The sum of the images cannot be represented as independent images because groups might overlap. Experiments E42 and E43 did not meet the conditions. E43 passed 11 out of 20 conditions in the test where 1,000 real and 1,000 AI generated images were used. There were 391 false alerts in original versions of real images and 490 false alerts in processed real images. E92 did not meet the acceptance rule and therefore did not reach the last evaluation phase. So, development results should not be confused with the last test phase (Keleş, 2026, E42,E49, E92 and E139).

Firstly several methods tried such as retraining all ready trained model (fine tunning) or change image tones to grey or making modifications on model scores. However, all the conditions were not met. After adding features of CLIP and DEAR and developing new pices that can learn from these features, E83 and E86 passed 17 out of 20 controls. E92 passed 20 of them. However, understanding and explaining explicitly what change made the model passed the controls cannot be determined. Because in every phase there were more than one changes. In addition passing 20 controls does not mean rule of detecting AI generated images also passed. In E92 weights of DINOv2, CLIP and DEAR weights did not changed only training the little pieces with the information that these models extract from image. The main goal was preserving AI detection rates while reducing the false alerts on real images. However, this needs to be tried on other datasets. Figure 2 shows that how the learned system connected the web demo.

Transfer learning means using what trained models learned previously and benefiting from them. Encoder transforms images into numerical information. This information was used to train little pieces. In addition weights of the encoder did not changed. Therefore, this method resulted in a more suitable workflow on this computer. DINOv2, CLIP or DEAR were not developed in this project. Only the information that these models extract from images was used to train little pieces. The system resulting from this method was evaluated and modified.

This table 3 shows the scorse that E92 got and includes 10 numerical condition for both image versions such as original image and processed image, so in total there are 20 conditions. This list created for this project these conditions are not mean universal standarts for image detection model.Some of the conditions are related to each other. Even if E92 passed all the conditions, but missed an AI genereted image which was detected by previous model. Therefore, passing all condtions does not mean full acceptance.

Figure 3 shows that compare results of two models in 160 real images. There are three key findings. First one is false alert on real images were dropped down 68 to 0. Second one is false alert of processed image dropped down 68 to 14. Third one is E92 detected 159 out of 160 in both original version and processed version of AI generated images. For both versions, 10 numerical conditions were determined, making 20 in total, and all were passed. However, E92 missed one original AI image which E43 had detected. In addition, there was a rule that a new model should not miss an AI image detected by the reference model. Therefore, E92 passed all 20 numerical conditions, but did not meet all the acceptance conditions.

This set have been used few times in separate experiments. This set includes ten real SIDD scenes and two different families. In addition, E102 performed 12 out of 160 false alerts in images which indicates that better performance than E92. Since E92 performed 14 out of 160 in false alerts in real images. However, E102 missed same AI generated image, so the model cannot be accapted.

section: 4.5.7 Honest scores and the web demostration
text: In the web demo 0-100 does not demonstrate that the probability of an image being AI generated. There are two thershold values that come from previous experiments. The first one is the upper bound which comes from E48 calibration. If the original images's score exceeds 7.94 or at this score demo gives AI alert. The second one is lower bound which comes from E49 calibration and development analysis. If both version of image ,original and processed, are below approximately 1.15 demo indicates that there are no clear signs to label as AI generated. Otherwise, the result is ambigous, which means demo cannot classify the image AI or real image. However, this is not mean that an image with no clear AI signs is definitely real

section: 4.5.7 Honest scores and the web demostration
text: In the same development dataset, out of 160 real images, 139 had no clear signs of being AI generated and 21 images were uncertain. There were no AI alerts on real images. Out of 160 AI generated images, the demo gave 159 AI generation alerts, but one image was uncertain. These results came from the web demo, which considered two versions of each image, original and processed. In the previous table, evaluation was done separately for both versions of the images. In addition, there were some controls that checked the uploading process and code flow. These controls checked software operation, not image detection accuracy (Keleş, 2026).

Photographs that comes from mostly same mobile phone and contains similar sceens were selected from my galary. And number of photoprahps were 206 and real image. Then conducting a test scores were like this. 9 fasle alerts in original version of image and there were 18 false alerts in processed version. In addition to this, this set cannot be considered as independent test and the last one since this development set used in development phase. (Keleş, 2026, E95).

While checking the training data there were reduced images to 224 pixel which are percentages were 29.18 for real , 7.68 for AI generated images. This encourged to think if these difference affecting model performance. However, no clear proof by selft. Then new candidate model which uses pixel structure features added. Results were better in non processed images but worse in processed images. In JPEG75 test AI detection rate reduced 75.73% to 74.15 therefore this rejected. After these experiments there was no enlighting answer that why model performance dropped down. However, the method dropped down the performance indendified. (Keleş, 2026, E148–E152). There is need to be conduct indepenedt test for this.
